lead: Two memory pictures cover most parallel machines. In a shared-memory machine, all processors use one address space, so a write by one core can be read by another. In a distributed-memory machine, each node has private RAM and nodes exchange messages. The first is common inside a server or chip; the second is common across servers, clusters and cloud data centres. The choice changes both hardware and programming style: threads and locks on one side, send and receive on the other.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for why parallel time matters, and Chapter 1.2 for SIMD and MIMD names.

blocks.text: A shared-memory machine gives every processor one view of memory. A load or store names an address, and any processor can use that address. The operating system and programs see one address space. This makes data sharing direct: write a value, and another processor can read it. It also makes locking and producer-consumer queues simpler than in a message-based machine.

The common form is UMA, uniform memory access, also called SMP, symmetric multiprocessing. All processors reach all memory banks in about the same time. Small systems join processors and memory with a bus. A bus is simple, but only one transfer can use it at a time. Larger systems use a crossbar, a switch that connects any processor to any memory bank; it gives more bandwidth and costs more wires.

items: UMA / SMP: one address space; similar latency to all RAM; bus or crossbar.
NUMA: each processor has local RAM; local access is faster; remote access crosses an interconnect and has higher latency. The address space is still one.
COMA: cache-only memory architecture; main memory is treated as a large cache and data migrates to where it is used. It is a research and specialized design form.

blocks.text: A cache stores copies of recently used lines. On a shared-memory machine, two caches may hold the same line. Cache coherence is the problem of keeping those copies consistent when one processor writes. That one line is enough here; protocols belong to Unit 5.

Shared-memory SIMD is another architecture form: many lanes run one instruction stream over different data, often with a shared control unit. The tree and mesh machines are network forms; see Chapter 1.5.

sections.h3: Distributed memory: private memory and messages

blocks.text: A distributed-memory machine is built from nodes. Each node has a processor, its own RAM, and a network interface. A node cannot load or store an address in another node's RAM. To share data, one node sends a message and another receives it. The address space is not shared. This is the main difference from a shared-memory machine.

A cluster is a set of complete computers joined by a network; each computer keeps its own operating system image in the usual case. An MPP, massively parallel processor, is a large machine designed for scale, often with a specialized interconnect and many nodes. Modern multicore nodes combine both ideas: inside a node, cores share RAM; across nodes, the machine passes messages.

The basic primitives are send and receive. send(destination, buffer) sends the bytes in buffer to a named destination. receive(source, buffer) waits for a message and copies it into buffer. A synchronous send waits until the receiver has taken the message, or at least until it is safe to reuse the buffer. An asynchronous send returns at once and lets the program do other work; the system completes the transfer later. Full protocols, matching and buffering are in Unit 4.

Message passing has a cost that shared memory hides: the sender must copy data into the network, the network carries it, and the receiver copies it out. Latency is the time for one small message; bandwidth is the bytes per second for large messages. Local shared-memory access is usually nanoseconds; a network message is often microseconds or more.

blocks.where: T_msg is the time for one message of n bytes; L is startup latency in seconds; B is bandwidth in bytes per second; T_copy is one local copy time in seconds.

blocks.text: The choice is not just hardware. Shared memory is easy for pointer-based data structures and fine-grained sharing. Message passing forces explicit data movement, so the programmer must partition data and schedule communication. That extra effort can pay back in scalability: a cluster can grow by adding nodes, while a bus-based SMP has a fixed limit and a large shared address space must be kept coherent.

blocks.text: Use shared memory inside one server or one multicore chip. Use distributed memory across servers, clusters and cloud regions. Many real systems are hybrid: OpenMP threads inside a node and MPI messages between nodes. Unit 3 covers those programming tools.

spec.aria: Two timelines. Four cores run a 20 second serial part then 20 seconds each, ending at 40 seconds. Two nodes run the serial part, 40 seconds each, then 10 seconds of messages, ending at 70 seconds.

examples.question: A job takes 100 s on one core. 20 s is serial and 80 s can run in parallel. (a) On a 4-core SMP with no message cost, find T4 and speedup S4. (b) On a 2-node cluster, the parallel part divides equally over 2 nodes and message overhead is 10 s; find T2node and speedup. (c) Which architecture is faster here?
steps: One-core time T1 = 100 s. Serial part = 20 s. Parallel part = 100 − 20 = 80 s.
(b) Cluster: T2node = serial + parallel/2 + overhead = 20 + 80/2 + 10 = 20 + 40 + 10 = 70 s. S2node = 100/70 = 1.428571... ≈ 1.43.
(c) 40 s < 70 s, so the 4-core SMP is faster in this model.
examples.answer: The 4-core SMP takes 40 s with speedup 2.5; the 2-node cluster takes 70 s with speedup 1.43, so the SMP wins here.

S2 = 100 / T2

print(round(S2, 2))

traps: Shared memory is not communication-free: NUMA remote access, bus contention and cache coherence all add time.
One address space does not mean one physical memory. In NUMA, local and remote RAM have different latencies.
A cluster is not the same as an SMP: nodes have private RAM; a thread cannot directly load a remote node's variable.
Speedup uses one-processor time in the numerator; do not divide by the number of cores when serial time is present.
Synchronous send does not always mean the receiver has read the data; it means the sender may safely continue or reuse the buffer under the stated rule.

quiz.a: UMA: all processors have about the same access time to all memory. NUMA: each processor has local memory with lower latency and can reach remote memory with higher latency, still in one address space.

quiz.q: Why must a distributed-memory program use send and receive instead of a normal load and store?
quiz.a: A node cannot address another node's private RAM. The only way to move data is for one node to send a message and the other to receive it.

quiz.q: A job takes 120 s on one core, with 30 s serial and 90 s parallel. Find T on a 3-core SMP with no overhead and the speedup.
A 4-core SMP has many coherence misses. A 2-node cluster has 25 s message overhead. What measurements decide which is faster for a given job?
quiz.a: Measure serial time, parallel time, coherence or contention cost on the SMP, and message latency plus copy cost on the cluster. Compare total times, not just core counts.
It is the requirement that multiple caches holding a copy of one memory line do not give different values after a write.

quiz.q: Give one reason message passing can scale beyond a bus-based SMP.
quiz.a: A cluster adds nodes and network links; a bus has one shared path and a single shared address space must be kept coherent.

quiz.q: Classify: (a) one chip with 8 cores sharing L3; (b) 64 PCs on Ethernet, each PC with 16 cores.
quiz.a: (a) Shared-memory multicore, UMA-like inside the chip with shared cache. (b) Hybrid distributed memory: message passing across PCs, shared memory inside each PC.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cloud systems use NUMA-aware placement and remote direct memory access (RDMA) to cut message cost. PGAS languages try to give a shared-memory view over distributed RAM, and GPU kernels use a small shared memory per block. Search for NUMA balancing, RDMA, PGAS and cache-coherent interconnects.
